| Term | Meaning |
|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Temp** | Air temperature in °C. |
| **RH** | Relative humidity in %. How "full" the air is with water vapour *at that temperature*. |
| **AH** | Absolute humidity in g/m³. The actual amount of water vapour in the air. |
| **Dew point** | The temperature at which the air would become saturated and condensation would start. |


# R

Load some packages

A package only needs to be **installed once**, but must be **loaded every session** with `library()`.

-   tidyverse: a family of useful packages for data analysis and plotting <https://tidyverse.org/>
-   ConSciR: functions for conservation science data <https://bhavshah01.github.io/ConSciR/index.html>


```{r eval=FALSE}
# Only run this ONCE if you get an error saying a package is "not found".
# (eval=FALSE means this chunk is skipped when you run the whole notebook.)
install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("readxl")
install.packages("curl")
install.packages("openair")
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("BhavShah01/ConSciR")
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse); library(ggplot2)
library(ConSciR) 
```

# Data

## Load some data

Download an Excel file from GitHub, save a copy on our computer, then read it into R.

`testdata <- read_excel("path/to/your_file.xlsx")`. Your data will need columns called `Date`, `Temp`, `RH` and `Sensor` to work with the ConSciR functions below.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(readxl)   # lets R read Excel files

# 1. The web address of the file
url <- "https://github.com/BhavShah01/ConSciR/raw/refs/heads/master/data-raw/mydata.xlsx"

# 2. What we want to call the file on our computer
destfile <- "mydata.xlsx"

# 3. Download it
curl::curl_download(url, destfile)

# 4. Read it into R and store it in an object called `testdata`
testdata <- read_excel(destfile)
```


#### Look at supplied dataset

**Always look at your data before you plot it.** These are quick ways of doing that.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# The first 6 rows
head(testdata)
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# glimpse() shows every column, its type, and the first few values.
# <dttm> = date-time, <dbl> = number, <chr> = text
glimpse(testdata)
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# How many rows? How many readings per sensor? What dates does it cover?
nrow(testdata)

testdata |>
  group_by(Sensor) |>
  summarise(
    Readings = n(),
    Start = min(Date),
    End = max(Date)
  )
```

### Check for missing data

Real sensors drop out, batteries fail. Missing values (`NA`) can quietly affect your results, so always check.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Count the number of NA (missing) values in each column
testdata |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))
```



# Graphs

## Basic graph

`graph_TRH()` is a ConSciR function that makes a quick time series of temperature and RH in one go.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
graph_TRH(testdata)
```

**Now the same idea built by hand with ggplot2.** Read it from top to bottom, each `+` adds a new layer:

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata |>                                  # start with the data
  ggplot() +                                 # create an empty plot
  geom_line(aes(Date, Temp), col = "red") +  # add a red line: x = Date, y = Temp
  geom_line(aes(Date, RH), col = "blue") +   # add a blue line: x = Date, y = RH
  labs(title = "Time Series") +              # add a title
  facet_grid(~Sensor) +                      # one panel per Sensor
  theme_classic()                            # a clean look
```

## Apply a theme

A **theme** changes the look of the graph (background, gridlines, fonts) but not the data. Try replacing `theme_classic()` with `theme_minimal()`, `theme_bw()`, `theme_light()` or `theme_dark()`.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
graph_TRH(testdata) + 
  theme_classic()
```

## Distributions: how are values spread out?

A **density chart** is a smoothed histogram. The higher the curve, the more readings at that value.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata |>
  ggplot() + 
  geom_density(aes(Temp), fill = "Red", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density(aes(RH), fill = "Blue", alpha = 0.5) + 
  labs(
    x = "Temperature and Humidity", 
    y = "Density", 
    title = "Density Chart") +
  facet_grid(Sensor~.) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Extra: histogram, one variable at a time

Plotting Temp and RH on a single x-axis (above) is convenient but a bit unusual. Separate plots are usually clearer.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata |>
  ggplot(aes(x = RH, fill = Sensor)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, colour = "white") +   # each bar covers 2% RH
  facet_wrap(~Sensor) +
  labs(title = "Histogram of RH", x = "RH (%)", y = "Number of readings") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Extra: boxplots to compare sensors

A **boxplot** summarises a distribution: the thick line is the median, the box is the middle 50% of readings, the "whiskers" show the typical range and any dots are unusual values (outliers).

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata |>
  pivot_longer(c(Temp, RH), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>  # stack Temp and RH into one column
  ggplot(aes(x = Sensor, y = Value, fill = Variable)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free_y") +      # separate y-axis for each variable
  labs(title = "Temperature and RH by sensor", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

> **Think about it:** Which sensor has the most stable conditions? Which has the biggest range?

## Relationship between Temp and RH

Does RH change when temperature changes? A **scatter plot** shows one point per reading.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Temp, y = RH)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +                              # small transparent points so overlaps are visible
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "red") +            # add a straight "line of best fit"
  facet_wrap(~Sensor) +
  labs(title = "Temperature vs RH", x = "Temp (°C)", y = "RH (%)") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# A single number summarising the relationship: the correlation coefficient.
#  +1 = perfect positive relationship, 0 = none, -1 = perfect negative relationship
testdata |>
  group_by(Sensor) |>
  summarise(Correlation_Temp_RH = round(cor(Temp, RH, use = "complete.obs"), 2))
```

> **Remember:** correlation does not mean causation. RH is partly *defined* by temperature (warm air can hold more water), so a strong negative correlation is physically expected.

## Bivariate chart

This is a ConSciR chart. Each hexagon/cell shows a third variable (here absolute humidity, `calcAH`) for each combination of Temp (x) and RH (y). The box shows a target comfort or conservation range.

Type `?graph_TRHbivariate` in the Console to see all the settings.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata |>
  add_time_vars() |>              # adds season, month, hour ... columns (explained in the Dates section below)
  graph_TRHbivariate(
    z_func = "calcAH",            # which variable to colour by
    LowT = 16, HighT = 25,        # target temperature range (°C)
    LowRH = 40, HighRH = 60,      # target RH range (%)
    Temp_range = c(0, 40),        # x-axis limits
    RH_range = c(0, 100),         # y-axis limits
    alpha = 0.7,
    limit_caption = "Bivariate Chart"
  ) + 
  facet_grid(Sensor ~ season)     # rows = Sensor, columns = season
```


## Psychrometric chart

A **psychrometric chart** is the standard engineers' chart for air. Temperature runs along the bottom, moisture content up the side, and curved lines show RH. Each point is one reading, coloured here by month.

Type `?graph_psychrometric` in the Console for the settings.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata |> 
  mutate(
    month = lubridate::month(Date, label = TRUE)   # make a column with the month name (Jan, Feb ...)
    )  |>
  graph_psychrometric(
    y_func = "calcAH",     # y-axis = absolute humidity
    data_col = "month") +  # colour the points by month
  facet_grid(~Sensor) + 
  theme_bw()
```

# Dates

Dates are the most useful (and most annoying) part of environmental data. The `lubridate` package makes them easier.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(lubridate)

# Pull the month out of the Date and add it as a new column
# NOTE: this only *displays* the result. We have not saved it, so `testdata` is unchanged.
testdata |>
  mutate(month = lubridate::month(Date, label = TRUE)) 
```

## Adding lots of date columns at once

`add_time_vars()` (from ConSciR) adds many handy columns in one step.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# We SAVE this one into a new object so we can reuse it below
testdata_time <- testdata |> 
  add_time_vars()

# See the new columns that were added
glimpse(testdata_time)
```

Useful new columns include `season`, `seasonyear`, `month`, `weekday`, `hour` and `day`. Use them to group and compare your data.

## Summary table by season

`group_by()` splits the data into groups, `summarise()` then calculates one row of results per group.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata |>
  add_time_vars() |>
  group_by(Sensor, seasonyear) |>                  # one group for every Sensor + season/year
  summarise(
    TempAvg = mean(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),            # na.rm = TRUE ignores missing values
    RHAvg = mean(RH, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

### Extra: a fuller summary table

Averages alone can hide a lot. Min, max and standard deviation (how much values vary) give a better picture.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata_time |>
  group_by(Sensor, season) |>
  summarise(
    Readings = n(),
    Temp_mean = mean(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    Temp_min  = min(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    Temp_max  = max(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    Temp_sd   = sd(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    RH_mean   = mean(RH, na.rm = TRUE),
    RH_min    = min(RH, na.rm = TRUE),
    RH_max    = max(RH, na.rm = TRUE),
    RH_sd     = sd(RH, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1)))   # round all numbers to 1 decimal place
```

## Daily averages

Raw sensor data can be very busy. Averaging by day reveals the longer-term pattern.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
daily <- testdata_time |>
  group_by(Sensor, day) |>
  summarise(
    Temp = mean(Temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    RH = mean(RH, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

daily |>
  pivot_longer(c(Temp, RH), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = day, y = Value, colour = Sensor)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(Variable ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Daily average Temp and RH", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Monthly patterns

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata_time |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = RH, fill = Sensor)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "RH by month", x = "Month", y = "RH (%)") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Time of day patterns

Is there a daily cycle (e.g. heating on in the morning, visitors in the afternoon)? A **heatmap** of hour of day against month can show this.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata_time |>
  group_by(Sensor, month, hour) |>
  summarise(Temp = mean(Temp, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = month, fill = Temp)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma") +       # a colour-blind friendly colour scale
  facet_wrap(~Sensor) +
  labs(title = "Average temperature by hour and month",
       x = "Hour of day", y = NULL, fill = "Temp (°C)") +
  theme_minimal()
```


```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata_time |>
  group_by(Sensor, month, hour) |>
  summarise(RH = mean(RH, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = month, fill = RH)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +       # a colour-blind friendly colour scale
  facet_wrap(~Sensor) +
  labs(title = "Average humidity by hour and month",
       x = "Hour of day", y = NULL, fill = "Humidity (%RH)") +
  theme_minimal()
```


```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Average daily cycle for each season, shown as a line
testdata_time |>
  group_by(Sensor, season, hour) |>
  summarise(RH = mean(RH, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = RH, colour = season)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~Sensor) +
  labs(title = "Average daily RH cycle", x = "Hour of day", y = "RH (%)", colour = "Season") +
  theme_bw()
```

# Is the environment within target?

Conservation guidelines often set a target range for conditions. Here we count how much of the time each sensor was inside the range used in the bivariate chart earlier (16-25 °C and 40-60 % RH). **Change the numbers to test other guidelines.**

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Define the target range once, so it is easy to change
low_T <- 16;  high_T <- 25
low_RH <- 40; high_RH <- 60

in_range <- testdata |>
  mutate(
    Temp_ok = Temp >= low_T & Temp <= high_T,    # TRUE if temp is within range
    RH_ok   = RH >= low_RH & RH <= high_RH,      # TRUE if RH is within range
    Both_ok = Temp_ok & RH_ok                    # TRUE only if both are
  )

# The mean of TRUE/FALSE values is the proportion of TRUE, so x 100 gives a percentage
in_range |>
  group_by(Sensor) |>
  summarise(
    `% time Temp in range` = round(mean(Temp_ok, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 1),
    `% time RH in range`   = round(mean(RH_ok, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 1),
    `% time both in range` = round(mean(Both_ok, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 1)
  )
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# The same information as a bar chart
in_range |>
  group_by(Sensor) |>
  summarise(
    Temperature = mean(Temp_ok, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    RH = mean(RH_ok, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    Both = mean(Both_ok, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-Sensor, names_to = "Target", values_to = "Percent") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Sensor, y = Percent, fill = Target)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +          # bars side by side
  labs(title = "Time within target range", x = NULL, y = "% of readings") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Calculating new variables from Temp and RH

ConSciR can calculate other useful properties from Temp and RH. `add_humidity_calcs()` adds several new columns at once (dew point `DP`, absolute humidity `AH`, mixing ratio `MR` and more).

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata_calcs <- testdata |>
  add_humidity_calcs()

# Compare Temp and RH with the new columns
testdata_calcs |>
  select(Date, Sensor, Temp, RH, DP, AH) |>
  head()
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Plot temperature and dew point together.
# When the dew point gets close to the temperature, condensation is likely.
testdata_calcs |>
  pivot_longer(c(Temp, DP), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Date, y = Value, colour = Variable)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Sensor, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Temperature and dew point", y = "°C", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

> **Think about it:** RH can swing up and down every day just because the temperature changes, even when the amount of water in the air has barely moved. Compare the plot of `RH` with the plot of `AH` (absolute humidity) to see this for yourself.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata_calcs |>
  pivot_longer(c(RH, AH), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Date, y = Value, colour = Sensor)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(Variable ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "RH vs absolute humidity", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Mould risk

`add_conservation_calcs()` adds conservation-focused columns, including a simple mould risk flag. Run `?add_conservation_calcs` to see what each column means.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
testdata_mould <- testdata |>
  add_conservation_calcs()

# What share of readings were flagged as a mould risk, for each sensor?
testdata_mould |>
  count(Sensor, Mould_risk) |>                   # count rows for each combination
  group_by(Sensor) |>
  mutate(Percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))   # turn counts into percentages
```
